nameStory: Red sand spurrey gets its name from its preference for sandy soils and its tiny pink flowers that often have a reddish tinge. The word 'spurrey' comes from an old European name for similar small, sprawling plants that were considered agricultural weeds. Despite its delicate appearance, this tough little plant thrives in the kind of sandy, disturbed ground that many other flowers avoid.
description: Red sand spurrey is a small, sprawling annual or perennial herb that forms low mats or cushions in sandy places. It rarely grows taller than 10 inches, with slender stems that branch out from the base and often lie flat against the ground. The plant produces numerous tiny pink flowers throughout the growing season, each about the size of a pinky nail. Its narrow, fleshy leaves and compact growth habit help it survive in dry, sandy conditions where larger plants struggle.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Five rounded pink petals form tiny flowers less than half an inch across, with fuzzy, sticky sepals (the green parts behind the petals) that feel glandular to the touch

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, thread-like leaves under an inch long that feel slightly thick and fleshy, often ending in a tiny sharp point, with shiny white papery stipules at the base

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats with slender stems that branch repeatedly and often sprawl along the ground, rarely exceeding 10 inches tall

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thin, often reddish stems that feel sticky or glandular when touched, especially near the flowers and growing tips

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny capsules split open to release dust-like reddish-brown seeds that cling to fingers when touched

habitat: Look for red sand spurrey in sandy, well-drained soils throughout New England, especially in disturbed areas like roadsides, construction sites, and sandy paths. It thrives in poor, dry soils where competition from larger plants is minimal, often appearing in coastal areas, railroad beds, and the sandy margins of parking lots. This adaptable plant can handle both full sun and light shade but always prefers loose, sandy ground.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as small rosettes of fleshy leaves, with first flowers appearing in late spring. The sticky, glandular feel of young stems becomes noticeable as temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with continuous small pink flowers from early summer through late summer. Plants form distinctive low mats that spread across sandy surfaces.
seasonality.fall: Flowering continues into early fall, with seed capsules becoming more prominent. Annual plants begin to turn reddish-brown while perennial forms may persist as green rosettes.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die back completely, but perennial forms may survive as small evergreen rosettes close to the ground in protected sandy spots.

funFact: Red sand spurrey's tiny seeds are so lightweight that a single plant can produce thousands of them, and they're designed to stick to anything that touches them - including the feet of insects, birds, and hikers - turning every passing creature into an unwitting seed disperser for colonizing new patches of sand.
confusionNotes: Red sand spurrey is most easily confused with other small pink flowers in sandy areas, but its combination of thread-like fleshy leaves, sticky glandular stems, and preference for pure sand sets it apart. Remember: if it's in sand and feels sticky, it's likely spurrey.
contextualKnowledge: Though called 'red' sand spurrey, the flowers are actually pink - the 'red' refers to the reddish tinge the whole plant often develops, especially the stems and seed capsules. This European native has become so well-established in sandy areas across New England that many people assume it's a native wildflower.
compareHints: Red sand spurrey differs from its relative saltmarsh sand spurrey by growing in dry sandy areas rather than salt marshes, and having smaller flowers with less fleshy leaves. Canada sand spurrey is much rarer and has larger flowers with white petals instead of pink. All three share the distinctive thread-like leaves and low, mat-forming growth habit typical of the sand spurrey family.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike Red Sand Spurrey which has distinctly pink flowers and grows in dry, non-salty areas, Saltmarsh Sand Spurry has white to very pale pink flowers and requires salty conditions.
Canada sand-spurry is the most cold-tolerant and northern of the three sand-spurries in New England.
